name: Fifty-one Japanese (Gojūichi)
description: Fifty-one Japanese (Gojūichi / äº”å ä¸€) is a popular fast-paced children's and social card game in Japan. A variation of the 'Commerce' family of games, it focuses on suit-based point collection. Players interact with a public pool of five cards on the table, swapping their own cards to reach a target score of 51. The game is known for its tension-filled ending, where one player can 'Stop' the game, giving everyone else only one last chance to improve their hand.

history.origins: Part of the global '51' family, which includes the Chinese Wǔshíyī Diǎn and various European variants. In Japan, it has transitioned from a gambling game into a staple family and childhood game.
timeline: Mid-20th Century: Becomes widely known across Japan as a schoolyard and family favorite.
1990s-Present: Frequently included in Japanese digital card game anthologies.
Modern Day: Shared as a 'quick game' (puchingu-gēmu) during social gatherings.
history.cultural: Commonly used to teach children addition (up to 51) and strategic suit-tracking.
history.evolution: The Japanese version streamlined the complex drawing rules of other variants, settling on a mandatory 'Exchange or Swap' mechanic that keeps the table cards rotating rapidly.

setup.dealing: Assign five cards to each player and place five cards face-up in the center of the table (the 'Market'). The remaining cards form the draw pile (used only when the table is cleared).

rules.objective: Assemble a 5-card hand of the same suit that totals exactly or as close to 51 as possible.
rules.gameplay:
Each turn (clockwise), a player MUST perform one of the following exchanges with the table:
1. 1-for-1: Swap one card from your hand for one card from the table.
2. 5-for-5: Swap your entire hand for all five cards on the table.
3. Stop: If you have a high score (usually 40+), you may say 'Stop'. This triggers the final round.
keyRules: Matching Suit constraint: Your score is only the total of cards within the SAME suit. If you have cards of different suits, you only count the suit that gives you the highest total.
Empty Market: If a 5-for-5 swap occurs, the next player may choose to 'Refresh the Market' by clearing the discarded hand and dealing five fresh cards from the deck.
Winning condition: Assemble a 5-card hand of the same suit that totals exactly or as close to 51 as possible.

strategy.basic: Identify the 'Power Suits' on the table. If you see the Ace of Hearts on the table, immediately start collecting Hearts.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Stop' Timing: Don't wait for 51. If you hit 45 or 48 early in the game, call 'Stop' immediately. Your opponents will likely have fragmented hands and won't be able to catch up in a single turn.
strategy.advanced: Market Manipulation: If you have a card that an opponent clearly needs (e.g., they are swapping for Spades and you hold the Spade King), keep it in your hand as long as possible. Only drop it to the table when you can simultaneously pick up a card that completes your own suit.
tips: Keep track of which suits other players are taking. If two people are collecting Diamonds, switch to Clubs or Spades to avoid competition.
A 5-for-5 swap is a great way to 'reset' a bad hand if the table has even two cards of a matching suit.

scoring.description: Collect 5 cards of same suit totaling as close to 51 as possible. Ace=11, K/Q/J=10, 2-10=face value. Exact 51 = instant win.
scoring.winCondition: Highest single-suit total when game stops (max 51). Exact 51 = instant win.

synthesis.shortDescription: A fast-paced Japanese collection game where players exchange cards with a central market to build a 5-card suit totaling 51, with a strategic 'Stop' mechanism.
